meta.title: Who really said "There may be a great fire in our soul, yet no one ever comes to warm themselves at it, and the passers-by see only a wisp of smoke coming from the chimney"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes, van Gogh. He wrote it in French to his brother Theo from Cuesmes, June 1880 (letter 155). The familiar English is a translator's wording, lightly altered.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There may be a great fire in our soul, yet no one ever comes to warm themselves at it, and the passers-by see only a wisp of smoke coming from the chimney'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine van Gogh: letter 155 to Theo, Cuesmes, June 1880, written in French. The popular English swaps two words from the Complete Letters translation.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Van Gogh wrote it in French to his brother Theo from Cuesmes in the Belgian Borinage, in the letter numbered 155 and dated between about 22 and 24 June 1880 — letter 133, dated July 1880, in the older Complete Letters numbering. The familiar English is a translator’s wording, and the version in circulation swaps two words: the 1978 Complete Letters text reads “warm himself at it” and “a wisp of smoke coming through the chimney.”

source.heading: The letter

docMeta.dd: Letter to Theo van Gogh, no. 155 (no. 133 in the older numbering)
Cuesmes, Belgium — between about 22 and 24 June 1880 (dated July 1880 in the Complete Letters)
French: “Tel a un grand foyer dans son âme et personne n’y vient jamais se chauffer…”
English wording from The Complete Letters of Vincent van Gogh, 2nd ed., vol. 1 (New York Graphic Society, 1978), p. 197

source.excerpt: Well, that’s how it is, can you tell what goes on within by looking at what happens without? There may be a great fire in our soul, but no one ever comes to warm himself by it, all that passers-by can see is a little smoke coming out of the chimney, and they walk on. All right, then, what is to be done, should one tend that inward fire, turn to oneself for strength, wait patiently — yet with how much impatience! — wait, I say, for the moment when someone who wants to comes and sits down beside one’s fire and perhaps stays on?
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traces the expression to van Gogh’s letter to Theo of 22–24 June 1880 (letter 155 in the Van Gogh Museum database), gives the French original, and reproduces the English from the 1978 Complete Letters, vol. 1, p. 197.
Wikiquote ↗ lists it in its sourced 1880 section, citing letter no. 155 as published in Vincent van Gogh – The Letters: The Complete Illustrated and Annotated Edition.
The WebExhibits online edition ↗ carries the surrounding paragraph under the older number, letter 133, Cuesmes, July 1880.
The volume Quote Investigator cites is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗: The Complete Letters of Vincent van Gogh, vol. 1, New York Graphic Society, Boston, 1978.
source.excerptNote: Quoted from the online edition of the letters at WebExhibits (letter 133, Cuesmes, July 1880), which credits the translation to Mrs. Johanna van Gogh-Bonger, edited by Robert Harrison. Note that it renders the sentence differently again from the widely circulated “wisp of smoke” line — a useful reminder that the English here is always a choice.

source.rightsNote: Van Gogh’s French original of 1880 is long out of copyright — he died in 1890. The English sentence people quote is not the original: it comes from The Complete Letters of Vincent van Gogh, an English translation first published in 1958 by the New York Graphic Society (the wording above is from the 1978 second edition, vol. 1, p. 197), so that translation remains in copyright in the United States. Quoting a sentence for commentary is ordinary fair use; reproducing the translated letters at length is not.

author.name: Vincent van Gogh
author.heading: Vincent van Gogh
author.bio: Van Gogh took a missionary posting at Petit-Wasmes in the coal-mining Borinage in January 1879, lived as poorly as the congregation he served, and was dismissed by the church authorities; he was still adrift in the spring of 1880 when he wrote the letter this line comes from. Later that year, at Theo’s suggestion, he began drawing the people around him in earnest and enrolled at the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts in Brussels. The roughly 900 surviving letters — most of them to Theo — are why so much of what the world quotes as “van Gogh” is writing rather than painting.

misattribution.heading: The attribution holds — the English drifted
misattribution.intro: This one is not a fake. Van Gogh wrote it, and the doubt worth having is about the wording, which is a translator’s choice several times over.

items.who: “warm themselves at it…coming from the chimney”
items.why: The English text Quote Investigator reproduces from The Complete Letters of Vincent van Gogh, 2nd ed., vol. 1, p. 197 reads “warm himself at it, and the passers-by see only a wisp of smoke coming through the chimney, and go along their way.” The circulating form quietly modernises the pronoun and drops the closing clause (Quote Investigator ↗).

items.who: “Someone has a great fire in his soul…”
items.why: Wikiquote’s sourced 1880 entry carries the Van Gogh Museum edition’s rendering — “Someone has a great fire in his soul and nobody ever comes to warm themselves at it, and passers-by see nothing but a little smoke at the top of the chimney and then go on their way” — the same French sentence, a different English one (Wikiquote ↗).
Quote Investigator records that the 2011 collection Black Cab Wisdom printed the line under Collins’s name, with van Gogh noted only parenthetically (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Van Gogh deserves full credit: he penned it in French, to Theo, in an 1880 letter — and every English version you have seen is somebody’s translation of it (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: A man asking to be seen
lead: The letter was written from a rented room in Cuesmes, in the Belgian coal country, after the church authorities had removed van Gogh from the missionary post he had taken at Petit-Wasmes in January 1879 — a stretch in which, by his family’s account, he was simply idle. The fire-and-chimney sentence is not a slogan about creative genius. It sits inside a passage asking a plainer and more painful question: whether anything true about a person is legible from the outside at all.

In the same paragraph he answers himself — tend the fire, wait, and hope someone sits down beside it. Later that year, on Theo’s suggestion, he began drawing the people around him in earnest, and by November 1880 he was enrolled at the academy in Brussels.
context.detailsSummary: He used the image more than once
detailsBody: Quote Investigator notes that van Gogh reached for the same fire metaphor again in a letter of December 1882, describing a great fire within an artist’s heart and studio — which is part of why the 1880 sentence reads as a settled conviction rather than a one-off flourish (Quote Investigator ↗).
